title: Making It Your Own
bigQuestion: How can you design a beat for a purpose, then use measurements to show it does what you planned?

story.title: A First Beat, Measured
story.kicker: Jada wanted a beat to help her class settle after lunch. Then she wanted proof it worked.
paragraphs: Jada's class came back from lunch loud and bouncy every day. Her teacher asked the class to design something to help everyone settle into reading time. Jada had one idea right away: a beat. A calm one, low and steady, that the class could breathe along with.

She opened the Drum Machine and set the tempo to 70 BPM, a little slower than a resting heart. She put a soft kick on the first beat of each bar and a quiet hi-hat on the off steps. No crash cymbals. No sudden sounds. She played it for her table. Two friends said it was too sleepy. One said it helped.

Jada wanted more than opinions. She played the beat into the Oscilloscope and looked at it. The kick drew slow, rounded waves. The hi-hat drew thin, fuzzy spikes. She checked that the loudest part was not too tall. She counted the time between kicks on the screen and got about 3.4 seconds, one full bar at 70 BPM.

Then she tested it. For one week the class heard her beat after lunch. For another week they did not. Each day, the teacher timed how long it took for the room to be ready to read. Jada had a claim, a plan and a way to measure. In this chapter, you will design and test a beat of your own.
story.think: What made Jada's project an investigation and not just a song? Name the parts.

lessons.title: Start With a Purpose
lessons.mainIdea: Good design starts with a clear purpose and a list of what the design must do.
reading: Engineers do not start by building. They start with a question: what is this for? Jada's purpose was to help a class settle. Another student might want a beat for a dance, for a workout, or for walking the dog. The purpose shapes every choice.

Next come the *criteria*, the things the design must do to succeed. For a calm beat, the criteria might be: slow tempo, steady pulse, no sudden loud sounds. Then come the *constraints*, the limits you must work within. Maybe you have only 16 steps, one bar, and five minutes.

Writing these down first saves time later. When you are not sure whether to add a crash cymbal, check the criteria. No sudden loud sounds? Then leave it out. Criteria also tell you what to measure when you test. Design and science meet here: a clear goal leads to a fair test.

words.d: the things a design must do to be a success
the limits a design must work within, such as time, tools or space

look.title: Two Purposes
look.text: Student A wants a beat for a school dance. Student B wants a beat to help people focus while reading.
look.prompt: Write two criteria for each beat. How are they different? What tempo might each one use?

check.q: What should a design start with?
check.why: Knowing the purpose shapes every choice.

check.q: Which is a criterion for a calm beat?
choices: Only one bar of steps allowed
Must be done in five minutes
Must be made on a Tuesday
check.why: Criteria describe success. The others are constraints or not relevant.

check.q: Having only 16 steps is an example of what?
check.why: A constraint is a limit you work within.

lessons.title: Build in Layers
lessons.mainIdea: Building a beat one layer at a time lets you hear what each part adds.
reading: Most producers build a beat in *layers*. Start with the kick drum alone and get it feeling right. Then add the snare. Listen. Then add the hi-hat. Listen again. Each layer should earn its place.

Building in layers is like adding one ingredient at a time when you cook. If the soup tastes wrong, you know what changed. If you add everything at once and it sounds messy, it is hard to tell which part is the problem. This is also how scientists build a *model*: start simple, then add parts.

Leaving space is part of the design too. A step with no sound is called a *rest*. Rests give the beat room to breathe, and they make the sounds around them stand out. A beat with every step filled can feel crowded. For many people, a beat with space in it is easier to listen to and to move with.

words.d: one part of a beat, such as the kick or the hi-hat, added on top of the others
a step or moment in music with no sound
a simple version of something that helps us understand or test it

look.title: Too Busy
look.text: A student fills every one of the 16 steps with a kick, a snare and a hi-hat all at once. Friends say it sounds like a washing machine.
look.prompt: What would you tell the student to try? Which layer would you start with and why?

check.q: Why build a beat one layer at a time?
choices: So you can hear what each part adds
So the beat is always faster
Because the machine only has one sound
check.why: Adding one layer at a time shows the effect of each part.

check.q: What is a rest in music?
choices: A step or moment with no sound
check.why: A rest is silence, and it gives the beat space.

check.q: A beat sounds messy. What does building in layers help you do?
choices: Find which part causes the problem
check.why: When you add one part at a time, you know what changed.

try.en: Try it on the Drum Machine
try.es: Pruébalo en la caja de ritmos

lessons.title: Change One Thing at a Time
lessons.mainIdea: To learn what a change does, change only one variable and keep everything else the same.
reading: Say your beat feels too rushed. You could change the tempo, move the snare, and turn off the hi-hat all at once. If it gets better, which change helped? You cannot tell. Change one thing at a time.

The thing you change on purpose is the *independent variable*. What you watch for is the *dependent variable*. Everything else you keep the same is a *controlled variable*. If you change the tempo from 90 to 80 BPM and ask three friends how calm it feels, tempo is independent, calmness is dependent, and the sounds and volume stay controlled.

This is the heart of a fair test. It works for beats, for plants, for medicine, for bridges. It is how Jada tested her beat: the same class, the same time of day, the same reading time, with and without the beat. Only one thing changed.

words.d: the one thing you change on purpose in a test
what you measure to see the effect of the change
something kept the same so the test is fair

look.title: Which Change Helped?
look.text: Sam changes his beat from 110 to 90 BPM, removes the snare and turns the volume down, all at once. His friends say it is much calmer now.
look.prompt: Can Sam say which change made it calmer? Plan a better test with only one change.

check.q: Why change only one thing at a time?
choices: So you know which change caused the result
Because machines allow only one change
check.why: One change at a time links the cause to the effect.

check.q: You change the tempo and measure how calm listeners feel. What is the tempo?
check.why: The tempo is what you changed on purpose.

check.q: In Jada's test, what was a controlled variable?
choices: The time of day the class heard it
How long the class took to settle
check.why: She kept the time of day the same so the test was fair.

lessons.title: Reading a Waveform
lessons.mainIdea: On an oscilloscope, you can read a sound's loudness from the height of the waves and its pitch from how close they are.
reading: Play your beat into the Oscilloscope. The line jumps each time a drum hits and settles back between hits. The picture is the beat's *waveform*. Reading it is like reading a graph: time runs left to right, and the height of the line shows the push and pull of the air.

Look for three things. First, how tall do the biggest waves get? That is the peak amplitude, the loudest moment. If the waves hit the top of the screen and flatten, the sound is *clipping*, too loud for the system, and it will sound harsh. Second, how quickly does each hit fade? That is its *decay*. Third, how far apart are the hits? That is the rhythm.

You can adjust the screen. Stretching the time scale lets you zoom in on one kick to see its individual wiggles. Squeezing it lets you see a whole bar. Changing the height scale lets you see quiet sounds. A good scientist chooses the scale that shows what they want to measure.

words.d: the shape a sound makes when it is drawn over time
when a sound is too loud for a system and the tops of its waves get cut flat
how quickly a sound fades after it starts

look.title: Flat Tops
look.text: A student turns her beat all the way up. On the Oscilloscope, the tops and bottoms of the kick's waves are cut flat, like a mesa. The kick now sounds crackly.
look.prompt: What is happening? What should she change, and what will the waveform look like after?

check.q: On a waveform, what does the height of the biggest wave show?
check.why: Height shows amplitude, so the peak is the loudest moment.

check.q: The tops of the waves are cut flat. What is this called?
check.why: Clipping happens when a sound is too loud for the system.

check.q: To see one kick drum's wiggles up close, what do you change?
choices: Stretch the time scale to zoom in
check.why: A stretched time scale spreads out a short moment so you can see detail.

lessons.title: Kick and Hi-Hat on the Screen
lessons.mainIdea: A kick drum draws slow, big waves, and a hi-hat draws fast, small, noisy ones, which matches how low and high they sound.
reading: Play a kick drum alone into the Oscilloscope. You see a few big, rounded waves spaced far apart, and then they fade. Those far-apart waves mean a *low frequency*, often around 50 to 100 Hz for a deep kick. Big height means strong amplitude.

Now play the hi-hat alone. The line turns into a thin, jittery smear with no smooth shape. A hi-hat is made of many *high frequencies* at once, jumbled together. Scientists call a jumble of many frequencies noise, even when it sounds nice. The hi-hat also fades quickly, so its decay is short.

Put them together, and you can see why a beat works. The kick fills the low end with big, slow energy. The hi-hat fills the high end with fast, light ticks. They do not crowd each other, because they live in different frequency ranges. Mixing engineers call this giving each sound its own space.

words.d: a slow vibration that sounds deep, like a kick drum or bass
a fast vibration that sounds bright or thin, like a hi-hat
a jumble of many frequencies at once with no single pitch

look.title: Match the Picture
look.text: Screen 1 shows a thin, jittery smear that lasts a very short time. Screen 2 shows four wide, rounded waves that shrink slowly.
look.prompt: Which screen shows the kick and which shows the hi-hat? Name two clues.

check.q: What does a kick drum look like on the Oscilloscope?
choices: Big, rounded waves spaced far apart
check.why: The kick is low frequency and strong, so its waves are wide and tall.

check.q: Why does the hi-hat look jittery?
choices: It is a single low note
It is many high frequencies mixed together
check.why: The hi-hat is a noisy mix of high frequencies.

check.q: Why don't the kick and hi-hat crowd each other in a mix?
choices: They are always at different volumes
They never play at the same time
The hi-hat is not a sound
check.why: Low kick and high hi-hat fill separate parts of the frequency range.

lessons.title: Timing Your Beat With Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: You can check a beat's tempo by measuring the time between hits and turning it back into BPM.
reading: Your drum machine says the tempo is 90 BPM. Is it? Scientists check. Play the beat into the Oscilloscope and measure the time from one kick to the next kick on the main beats. That is the beat's *period*.

Turn the period back into tempo: BPM equals 60 divided by the period in seconds. If the kicks are 0.67 seconds apart, 60 divided by 0.67 is about 90. The measurement agrees with the setting. If you measure 0.60 seconds instead, the tempo is really 100 BPM, and something is set differently than you thought.

You can also check the steps. At 90 BPM, each of the 16 steps should last about 0.167 seconds. With swing on, the pairs of steps will not be equal; the first one will be longer. Measuring lets you see swing as numbers, not just a feeling. Record your measurements in a *data table*, with the setting in one column and the measured value in the next.

words.d: the time it takes for one full wave or one beat to pass
a chart with rows and columns for recording measurements

look.title: Measured Time Between Kicks
look.cite: Expected values worked out as 60 divided by BPM, rounded
look.prompt: Work out the BPM from each period. Do they match the settings? What would you measure at 75 BPM?

check.q: Kicks are 0.5 seconds apart. What is the tempo?
check.why: 60 divided by 0.5 is 120 BPM.

check.q: What is the rule for turning a period into BPM?
choices: BPM equals 60 divided by the period in seconds
BPM equals 16 divided by the period
check.why: There are 60 seconds in a minute, so divide 60 by the seconds per beat.

check.q: With swing on, what would you measure for a pair of steps?
choices: The first step is longer than the second
check.why: Swing stretches the first step of each pair.

lessons.title: Protect Your Hearing While You Create
lessons.mainIdea: When you make music, keep volume moderate, take breaks and check your levels so your ears last a lifetime.
reading: Making beats can mean hours in headphones. That is exactly when hearing damage can sneak up, because it does not hurt. Keep the volume at a comfortable level. A good check: if someone an arm's length away has to shout for you to hear them, it is too loud.

Take *listening breaks*. Every hour or so, take off the headphones for a few minutes. Your ears get tired, and tired ears hear less detail. After a break, you will often notice things in your beat you missed. Producers call these fresh ears.

Everyone's comfort level is different. Some people find certain sounds, like sharp hi-hats or sudden crashes, painful or overwhelming. That is useful information for a designer. It is fine to turn those sounds down, choose softer ones, or wear ear defenders. A beat that works for more people is a better design.

words.d: time away from headphones or loud sound so the ears can rest
how loud a sound is set to play

look.title: The Arm's-Length Check
look.text: Leo wears headphones while making a beat. His friend stands an arm's length away and talks in a normal voice. Leo does not hear him at all.
look.prompt: What does this tell Leo? What two things should he do?

check.q: Why can hearing damage from headphones be hard to notice?
choices: It always happens in one second
check.why: Noise damage often happens without pain, so habits matter.

check.q: What are fresh ears?
choices: Rested ears that notice more after a break
check.why: After a listening break you hear more detail.

check.q: A classmate finds sharp hi-hats painful. What is a good design choice?
choices: Make them louder so they get used to it
Turn them down or use softer sounds
check.why: Designing for more people's comfort is better design.

lessons.title: Samples, Credit and Fairness
lessons.mainIdea: When you use a sound someone else made, give them credit and follow the rules for using their work.
reading: A *sample* can mean a single measurement, but in music it also means a piece of another recording used in a new song. Hip hop was built on samples: a drum break from a funk record, a horn line from a jazz record, looped and flipped into something new.

The sounds in those old records were made by real people: drummers, singers, engineers. Their work is protected by *copyright*, a law that gives creators rights over how their work is used. Professional musicians who sample a song usually ask permission and often pay the people who made it. This is called clearing a sample.

For school projects, you can use the sounds built into the Drum Machine, record your own sounds, or use sounds that are marked free to use. Either way, give *credit*: write down where each sound came from. Scientists do the same when they cite other people's data. Credit is how we show respect for the work we build on.

words.d: in music, a piece of a recording reused in a new piece
a law that gives creators rights over how their work is copied and used
saying clearly who made something or where it came from

look.title: The Borrowed Horn
look.text: A student loops a horn part from a famous song in his beat. He posts it online. Someone asks who played the horn part.
look.prompt: What should the student have done before posting? How is this like a scientist citing data?

check.q: What is a music sample?
choices: A free trial of an app
A piece of a recording reused in a new piece
check.why: In music, a sample is borrowed from another recording.

check.q: What does copyright protect?
choices: A creator's rights over how their work is used
check.why: Copyright gives creators rights over copying and use.

check.q: How are giving credit in music and in science alike?
choices: Both show where the work you built on came from
check.why: Credit, in music or science, names the source.

lessons.title: Explain Your Beat Like a Scientist
lessons.mainIdea: A strong explanation makes a claim, backs it with measured evidence and uses science to explain why.
reading: You designed a beat. You measured it. Now share it the way scientists share their work: with a *claim*, *evidence* and *reasoning*. The claim is one sentence saying what your beat does. For example: my beat helps our class settle faster after lunch.

The evidence is what you measured. Jada's class took an average of about 6 minutes to settle without the beat and about 4 minutes with it, over one week each. Her oscilloscope showed no clipping and a steady 70 BPM. Evidence is numbers and observations, not just feelings, though listeners' comments count as evidence too if you collect them fairly.

The reasoning explains why the evidence supports the claim, using science. A steady pulse is easy for the brain to predict. A slow tempo is near a resting heart rate. No sudden loud sounds means nothing startles. Honest scientists also say what they are not sure of: one class, two weeks, and other things might have changed too.

words.d: a one-sentence statement that answers a question
measurements and observations that support a claim
the science that explains why the evidence supports the claim

look.title: Weak or Strong?
look.text: Explanation A: My beat is calm because it just is and I like it. Explanation B: My beat is calm. It runs at 70 BPM, has no sudden sounds and never clips on the Oscilloscope. Five of six listeners rated it calm. A slow, steady pulse is easy to predict.
look.prompt: Which explanation is stronger? Point to the claim, the evidence and the reasoning.

check.q: What is the evidence in a scientific explanation?
check.why: Evidence is what you measured and observed.

check.q: Which is a claim?
choices: Five of six listeners rated it calm
My beat helps our class settle faster
Steady pulses are easy to predict
check.why: A claim answers the question in one sentence. The others are evidence or reasoning.

check.q: Why should Jada mention it was only one class for two weeks?
choices: To make the beat sound better
Honest scientists name the limits of their evidence
check.why: Naming limits helps others judge how strong the evidence is.

choices: The things a design must do to succeed
The limits you must work within
The sounds in a drum machine
review.why: Criteria define success; constraints are the limits.

review.q: Why build a beat in layers?
choices: To hear what each part adds
review.why: One layer at a time shows each part's effect.

review.q: You change only the tempo and measure how calm listeners feel. What is calmness?
review.why: Calmness is what you measure in response.

review.q: The tops of a waveform are cut flat. What should you do?
review.why: Flat tops mean clipping. Lowering the level fixes it.

review.q: Which sound draws big, slow, rounded waves?
review.why: The kick is low frequency and strong.

review.q: Kicks on the main beats are 1.0 second apart. What is the tempo?
Which is a good hearing habit while making beats?
choices: Keep the volume at the maximum
review.why: Breaks rest the ears and give fresh ears.

review.q: What should you do when you use someone else's sound?
choices: Change its tempo so no one knows
Give credit and follow the rules for using it
review.why: Credit and permission respect the creator's work.
